long.title: What If You Could Fly For 10 Minutes A Day?
long.rel: Rio and his older sister Dana, a volunteer search and rescue climber in Colorado (supporting: Brett, an energy drink marketing boss).
long.rule: Rio can fly for only ten minutes a day in total; when the ten minutes run out, the lift fades over thirty seconds and he drops.
long.plant: Dana gives Rio her old beeping hiking watch and her 'halfway rule': when half your time is gone, you turn toward home.
long.choice: Fly the last four minutes to the finish line and the million dollars... or turn around at the halfway beep and dive for the ledge.
long.script: Two thousand feet above a red rock canyon, the wind is so loud you can't hear yourself breathe. The helmet camera on your head is streaming to four million people. Four... million. Below you, the river looks like a silver thread. Ahead of you, on the far rim, is a giant orange banner. Finish line. Cross it, and the check is one million dollars. On your wrist, an old plastic watch counts the seconds. Six minutes gone. Four left. Then your earpiece crackles. It isn't the sponsor. It's the park radio. A storm is rolling in from the west, and a teenage hiker is stuck on a ledge halfway down the canyon wall. The rangers can't reach her for an hour. The rain will reach her in ten minutes. You could get there in one. But four minutes is not a lot of sky. Can you do both? Should you even try? Rewind half a year. Your name is Rio. You deliver mail in a small mountain town in Colorado. And six months ago, on a frozen Tuesday, you slipped on an icy porch step... and didn't land. You just hovered there. Six inches off the ground. Holding a stack of catalogs. Humans were never built to fly. A bird's chest muscles can make up about a quarter of its body weight. Its bones are hollow, braced inside like a bridge. Even so, the heaviest flying birds top out around forty pounds. You weigh one hundred seventy. And yet... here you are. There's just one rule. You get ten minutes of flight a day. Ten minutes total. Not ten minutes per flight... ten minutes, period. When the time runs out, the lift fades over about thirty seconds, like a balloon losing air. If you're still up high when it's gone... gravity takes over. So what if you could fly for ten minutes a day? First, the fun part. Your mail route used to take six hours of winding mountain roads. Now? You skip the switchbacks. You hop from ridge to ridge, dropping letters on porches like a very polite owl. Mrs. Kowalski on Pine Street waves her coffee mug at you every morning. You wave back... from her roof. Upside: you see sunrise from above the clouds. Every... single... day. The world goes pink and gold, and the mountains poke through the clouds like islands. Downside: it's freezing up there. Air temperature drops about three and a half degrees Fahrenheit for every thousand feet you climb. Climb ten thousand feet, and a nice sixty degree morning becomes a twenty-five degree wind tunnel. Your eyebrows grow icicles. Downside: the air gets thin. At ten thousand feet, every breath holds roughly thirty percent less oxygen than at sea level. Climb too fast, and your head pounds, your fingers tingle, and your thoughts get slow and silly. Upside: the geese have accepted you. Mostly. Your older sister Dana is the only one who knows. She's a climber and a volunteer with the county search and rescue team. When you first showed her, she didn't scream. She didn't faint. She folded her arms. How long can you stay up? Ten minutes, you tell her. Total. She pulls an old black watch off her wrist. It's scratched and ugly, and it beeps like an angry microwave. She sets it to count down from ten. Then she taps it twice. Halfway rule, Rio. When half your time is gone, you turn toward home. No matter how close the summit looks. Why? Because the mountain doesn't care how close you got. You roll your eyes. She's been saying that since you were nine years old and she dragged you up your first peak. Half your water, half your daylight, half your energy... turn around. You wear the watch anyway. Then you make one mistake. A kid in town films you gliding past the water tower. The clip hits the internet. Ten million views by lunch. People call you the Flying Mailman. Strangers drive in from three states away just to watch your route. Your boss is not thrilled. Neither are the actual pilots. Birds and aircraft collide thousands of times a year in America, and now the airport has to add you to the list. A man in a glossy jacket shows up at the post office. His name is Brett. He runs marketing for a giant energy drink company. He doesn't waste time. Rio... one flight. One canyon. One mile across, live on the internet. Cross the finish line in under ten minutes, and we pay you one million dollars. Plus a lifetime supply of... well, energy drinks. One million dollars. That's more than you'd earn delivering mail for twenty years. Your mom's medical bills? Gone. Your crumbling truck? Gone. Dana's old car that only starts on weekdays? Gone. Now zoom out. What if everyone on Earth could fly ten minutes a day? Traffic would melt away... for about ten minutes. Then millions of people would be stuck halfway somewhere, waiting until tomorrow. Rooftops would become parking lots. Air traffic control would quit... immediately. And the sky? Busier than a mall on Black Friday. Back to your canyon. Brett's team plans everything. The route. The cameras. The drones. Your flight path is exactly one mile, rim to rim, with a few loops in the middle to please the crowd. Your best speed is about forty miles an hour. Without loops, you'd cross in under two minutes. With loops? Brett wants it close. Close is exciting. Close... sells drinks. Dana hates it. She shows up the night before, sits on your porch steps, and stares at the stars. You know the scariest words in the mountains, Rio? I'm almost there. She's carried people off peaks who were almost there. People who ignored the clock because the top looked so close. She doesn't tell you not to go. She just says one thing. Wear the watch. Halfway rule. Promise me. You promise. The morning of the flight, the sky is blue and perfect. Fifty thousand people line the rim. Food trucks. Drones. A guy dressed as a pigeon. You launch, and the crowd roars. You loop. You dive. You skim the river so close the spray hits your face. Brett is shouting in your earpiece. Higher! Bigger! The chat is exploding! Three minutes. Four. Five... Then the old watch on your wrist gives one sharp beep. Halfway. You'd almost forgotten you set it. That's when the park radio cuts in. That's when the clouds turn black in the west. And that's where we started. Two thousand feet up. Four minutes left. A finish line ahead... and a teenage hiker trapped on a ledge somewhere below. Brett is in your ear. Rio, keep going. The rangers will handle it. You're two minutes from a million dollars. The finish banner flaps in the wind. Close. So close. And somewhere in your head, Dana's voice. I'm almost there. You look down. The ledge is six hundred feet below the rim, on the wrong side of the canyon. Getting there takes one minute. Climbing back out with a passenger? Two more, maybe. The finish line would be gone. If you're too slow... you'll both run out of sky on the side of a cliff. One choice. Two directions. Fly the last four minutes to the finish line and the million dollars... or turn around at the halfway beep and dive for the ledge. You turn around. Brett's voice goes up an octave. You rip the earpiece out. The wind roars. The first raindrops sting like gravel. And there she is. A girl in a yellow raincoat, maybe sixteen, pressed flat against the rock, crying. Water is already pouring over the ledge above her like a faucet. You land beside her. Hey. I'm Rio. I deliver mail. Today, I deliver you. She laughs through her tears. You wrap your arms around her. One hundred sixty extra pounds. The lift strains. You rise... slowly... like an elevator with too many people in it. Halfway up, the watch beeps again. One minute left. Then thirty seconds. The lift starts to fade. You can feel it sinking out of you. Twenty feet below the rim, you're barely moving. Ten feet. And then... a hand. A rope. A harness. Dana. She's anchored to a boulder at the top of the cliff, soaking wet, leaning out over the edge. She heard the call on her own radio and drove like a maniac. Grab it! You do. The power dies a second later. For a moment, you and the girl swing from Dana's rope, with nothing under you but six hundred feet of rain. Then three rangers haul you over the lip, one pull at a time. The girl's name is Ava. She hugs Dana first. Then you. Then Dana again. Brett finds you at the trailhead. You didn't finish, he says. No, you say. I turned around. He stares at the phone in his hand. Then he turns it toward you. The livestream didn't cut out. Four million people watched you leave the finish line. Twenty million have watched it since. The comments say the same thing over and over. He turned around. Brett sighs. We're not paying you a million dollars. Pause. But the company wants to donate it. To search and rescue. In your name. Dana's team gets a new truck, new radios, and a helicopter fund. You get a framed photo of a man in a pigeon costume, crying at the finish line. And you still deliver the mail. Ten minutes a day. You always turn at five. So is any of this real? Not the floating... no human can lift off by wishing. But people keep trying, and they're getting close. In 1988, a pedal-powered aircraft called Daedalus flew about seventy-two miles from Crete toward the island of Santorini. One cyclist. No engine. Just legs. Today, wingsuit pilots can glide forward about three feet for every foot they drop, and reach speeds over one hundred miles an hour. And in 2019, inventor Richard Browning set a Guinness record in a jet-powered suit... flying about eighty-five miles an hour. So humans can fly. We just need a machine... or a cliff... or a very brave pilot. Here's what scientists still find strange, though. Flying is one of the most common dreams people report, all over the world. People who have never been in a plane still dream they're gliding above rooftops. Why does your brain keep rehearsing a skill your body has never had? So, real or not? Tell us where you'd fly first with your ten minutes, and who would be your Dana. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!
long.facts:
- Bird flight muscles can be about a quarter of body weight; hollow, braced bones
- Heaviest flying birds around 40 pounds
- Air cools about 3.5 F per 1,000 feet of climb
- At 10,000 feet each breath holds roughly 30% less oxygen than at sea level
- Thousands of bird and wildlife strikes with aircraft each year in the US
- Daedalus human-powered aircraft flew about 72 miles from Crete toward Santorini in 1988
- Wingsuits glide about 3 feet forward per foot dropped, over 100 mph
- Richard Browning jet suit Guinness speed record 2019, about 85 mph
- Flying dreams are among the most commonly reported dream themes
long.check:
- Bird flight muscle share (often cited 15-25%)
- '30% less oxygen at 10,000 feet' (effective oxygen ~31% lower)
- Browning record speed 136.9 km/h (85 mph), 2019
- Daedalus distance ~72 miles (115 km)

long.title: What If You Could Turn Invisible?
long.rel: Rio and his sixteen-year-old brother Nico, who feels invisible at his new school (supporting: Dez, Rio's old friend with a risky plan).
long.rule: Rio can stay invisible for up to one hour a day, but light passes through his eyes too, so the longer he is invisible the blurrier and grayer his sight becomes.
long.plant: Rio and Nico have a secret family knock from childhood: three knocks, a pause, then two.
long.choice: Lift the diamond and walk out unseen... or turn visible, hit every light, and be seen standing beside an open case.
long.script: The bakery on your corner opens at five. You walk in at four fifty-nine. Nobody sees you. You leave a five dollar bill on the counter, take one warm cinnamon roll, and walk out. The baker finds the money and stares at the door. It never opened. Okay... it did. He just didn't see who opened it. On the bus, a man is shouting into his phone about a business deal. You lean very close to his ear and whisper. Indoor voice. He drops the phone in his coffee. He hasn't said a word since. And at the dog park, your neighbor's golden retriever, Biscuit, runs straight up to an empty patch of air... and starts wagging. Dogs know. Dogs always know. Your name is Rio. You work night security at a natural history museum in Chicago. Dinosaurs, gemstones, a stuffed elephant named Gerald. And two months ago, during a thunderstorm, you looked down at your hands... and they weren't there. To understand how strange that is, think about how you see anything at all. Light bounces off an object and lands in your eyes. If that light gets blocked, absorbed, or bounced back, the object is visible. You're visible because your skin, blood and bones block light. Now, every bit of light passes straight through you. It doesn't bend. It doesn't stop. You're not see-through like glass. You're simply... not there. But there's a catch. And it's a big one. Inside your eye, a layer of cells called the retina catches light. That's how you see. To catch light, it has to stop light. An invisible retina can't do that. So the more invisible you get... the blinder you become. At first, your vision just turns a little gray. After twenty minutes, it's like looking through wax paper. After an hour, you can barely tell day from night. That's your rule. One hour a day. And the clock is your own eyes. So what if you could turn invisible? Upside: you never wait in a line again. Not at the DMV. Not at the airport. Not even at the deli counter on a Saturday. Downside: you never get served, either. You can't order a sandwich when the guy can't see you. Upside: no more awkward small talk with your landlord in the elevator. Downside: elevator doors close on you all the time. Every... single... time. Upside: you finally learn what your coworkers say about you when you're not around. Downside: you learn what your coworkers say about you when you're not around. Turns out, Brenda from the gift shop thinks your mustache looks like a sad caterpillar. You shave it that night. Is that a superpower... or a curse? And clothes are a problem. Your body vanishes. Your jacket doesn't. So you either walk around as a floating jacket... or you walk around wearing nothing at all in a Chicago winter, where January can drop below zero. Guess which one you pick? You keep a gym bag of clothes in your locker, change fast, and hope nobody ever opens that locker... and finds a uniform still warm with no one inside it. Here's another surprise. You're not totally invisible to everything. Your body still makes heat. A thermal camera would see a warm, glowing person-shaped blob walking around. Snakes like pit vipers can sense that kind of heat. So can the museum's security system... if you ever tripped it. You never have. At home, you live with your little brother Nico. He's sixteen. Your parents work in another state, so it's mostly the two of you, a toaster that sets off the smoke alarm, and a cat who refuses to be named. Nico just started at a big new high school. Three thousand students. He told you yesterday that nobody even knows his name yet. He said it like a joke. It wasn't a joke. You know the feeling. You used to be the quiet kid too. When you were little, you two invented a secret knock. Three knocks. Pause. Two knocks. It meant it's me, open up. You used it on bedroom doors, on the bathroom door, on the car window when Mom forgot you at soccer practice. Nico still uses it. Every morning, on your door, three... two. Even when you're awake. Even when you're already standing there. You never told him... it's your favorite sound in the house. Then Dez shows up. Dez was your best friend in high school. Funny, fast, always in trouble. He drives a car nicer than your apartment. He buys you dinner at a steakhouse and leans across the table. I know about the... thing, Rio. I saw you in the museum security footage. Or rather... I didn't. How? You don't ask. Dez has a plan. The museum's mineral hall holds a blue diamond. Forty-five carats. Insured for more money than you could earn in five lifetimes. Your shift. Your keys. Your power. Twenty minutes, Dez says. In and out. The cameras see an empty room. Nobody gets hurt. You get half. Nobody gets hurt. You hear that line in your head all night. Would anybody really get hurt? It's insured. It's just a rock. And half would mean Nico's college. Your parents could come home. Your toaster could finally retire. You tell Dez you'll think about it. It sits in your head all week... like a stone in your shoe. Now picture something wilder. What if a whole city could turn invisible? Crime would go up... at first. Then cities would switch to heat cameras, pressure sensors, and dogs. Lots of dogs. Biscuit would get a badge. And fashion would be ruined forever. Who cares about shoes nobody can see? The night of the plan arrives. Thursday. Storm warning. Dez texts you one word. Now. You walk into the mineral hall and switch on your power. The world fades to gray. You count. Five minutes. Ten. The glass case is right in front of you. The diamond glows like a little piece of ocean. Your key turns in the lock. Click. And then... the fire alarm. Lightning hit the old wiring in the dinosaur wing. You can smell it. Smoke is rolling down the main hallway like fog off a lake. The sprinklers on that side haven't kicked in yet. Your radio crackles. It's the front desk. Rio, there's a kid in the building. Says he's your brother. He came to bring you dinner. Then the lights go out. And you've been invisible for twenty-two minutes. Your eyes are wax paper. The smoke makes it worse. Gray on gray on gray. You can't see your own feet. Somewhere in that smoke is Nico. He doesn't know where to go. Tonight, he's the invisible one. Dez's voice buzzes through your earbud. Grab it and walk, Rio. Nobody will ever know you were there. Do you? If you stay invisible, nobody will ever see you holding a stolen diamond. But you can't see anything either. And Nico can't see you. If you turn visible, your eyes come back... and so do the cameras. They'll see you, the open case, the diamond, everything. It comes down to this. Lift the diamond and walk out unseen... or turn visible, hit every light, and be seen standing beside an open case. You let go of the power. Your body comes back first. Then your eyes. Color rushes in like someone turned the world back on. The smoke is thick, but now you can see the shape of it. You lock the case with shaking hands. Then you run. Nico! Nothing. Only alarms. Only smoke. You hit the emergency lights, and the hallway flickers red. Every camera in the building turns to look at you. Fine. Let them look. NICO! Then you hear it. Somewhere in the dark. Knock, knock, knock. Pause. Knock, knock. It's coming from the elephant hall. You'd know that knock anywhere. You crawl low, under the smoke, where the air is cleaner. Knock, knock, knock... knock, knock. Gerald the elephant looms out of the gray. And there's Nico, crouched beside him, rapping on the glass of a display case, coughing, holding a bag of burgers. I didn't know where you were, he says. So I knocked. You grab his hand. Together you crawl to the fire exit and spill out into the rain just as the trucks arrive. The firefighters put out the wiring fire in fifteen minutes. Nobody is badly hurt. Gerald smells like a campfire forever. The next morning, the museum director calls you into her office. She's watched every camera. She saw you open the case. She saw you lock it again. She saw you hit the lights and run straight into the smoke. And she saw a man in a parking garage, checking his phone, waiting for something that never came. She's already called the police about him. Then she does something you don't expect. She promotes you. Head of night security. Dez texts you once more. Just two words. You're boring. You block his number. That weekend, you go with Nico to his school's open gym night. He's quiet at first. Then he makes one basket. Then three. By the end of the night, a kid yells, Nice shot, Nico! He hears his own name in a gym full of strangers. He grins all the way home. And on Monday morning, there's a knock on your door. Three, then two. You open it. You don't go invisible much anymore. Maybe once a month. Just to check on Biscuit. But something has been bugging you. Last night, while you were invisible, you saw something no one else could. A gray shape, standing perfectly still in the dinosaur hall. Watching you. When you blinked... it was gone. Is there someone else in this city who can disappear? Would you have taken the diamond, or the knock? Tell us honestly in the comments, and tell us the secret signal your family uses. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!
long.facts:
- We see objects because they block, absorb or reflect light
- The retina must absorb light to see, so a truly invisible eye would be blind
- Body heat would still show on thermal cameras; pit vipers sense infrared heat
- Dogs rely heavily on smell and would still detect an invisible person
- Staying low under smoke gives cleaner air during a fire
long.check: - None critical; no specific statistics beyond story details

long.title: What If You Could See Through Walls?
long.rel: Rio and his wife Maya, a radiology technologist who is seven months pregnant (supporting: Gus Lane, host of a treasure-hunting TV show).
long.rule: Rio's sight works by sending a faint X-ray beam from his eyes, so every second he looks through something gives it a small dose; he wears a dosimeter badge and must stop when it turns red.
long.plant: Maya clips her old dosimeter badge on Rio and teaches him the radiation safety rule: time, distance, shielding.
long.choice: Stare into the rubble as long as it takes, while the cameras roll... or blink, step back, and do it Maya's way.
long.script: The warehouse roof caves in at nine fifteen. A wall of dust rolls across the TV set. The lights swing. Somebody screams. And under a pile of broken bricks, a man is trapped. You can't see him with normal eyes. But you don't have normal eyes. You can see through brick. Through steel. Through ten feet of rubble. Three cameras are pointed at your face. The host of the show is yelling, Rio, find him! Find him live! On your shirt, a little plastic badge has turned orange. Almost red. If you keep looking, you'll find the man in seconds. But every second you look, the man gets a dose of radiation from your eyes. So does everyone behind him. So does the rescuer kneeling right next to him. How long can you stare? Rewind a little. Your name is Rio. You're a home inspector in New Orleans. You crawl through attics and squeeze under porches, looking for rot, leaks and termites. Your wife, Maya, is a radiology technologist. She takes X-rays at the hospital. And she's seven months pregnant with your first baby. Six weeks ago, you were checking an old shotgun house in the Bywater. You stared at a water stain on the wall... and the wall melted away. Pipes. Wires. A family of very surprised mice. You could see through it. Here's how normal sight works. Visible light bounces off walls. That's why walls look solid. X-rays are a different kind of light. They carry much more energy. They slide through soft things like skin and wood, and get blocked by dense things, like bone and metal. That's why an X-ray of your hand shows the bones but not the skin. There's just one problem. The world doesn't have many X-rays floating around for you to see. So your eyes make their own. When you focus, a faint beam shoots out of your eyes, passes through the wall, and comes back. Walls don't care. People... should. X-rays can damage cells. One quick look is tiny. A long stare is not. Maya figures it out before you do. She puts her old dosimeter badge on your shirt. Radiation workers wear these every day. They track how much exposure you've had. Green means fine. Orange means slow down. Red means you're done for the day. Then she taps your forehead and says the three words every X-ray tech learns on day one. Time, distance, shielding. Less time looking. More distance away. Something heavy in between. That's your rule now. And you'll need it. So what if you could see through walls? Week one, your job gets easy. You find a cracked pipe inside a wall without cutting a single hole. You spot termites chewing through a beam... and the homeowner nearly hugs you. You find a lost wedding ring under the floorboards. And a time capsule from 1952 in a chimney. It contains a baseball card, a love letter, and a very old peanut butter sandwich. Upside: you never lose your keys again. You just look through the couch. Downside: you see things you can't unsee. Your neighbor's bathroom. Your boss's hidden candy drawer. Your own skeleton in the mirror every morning, waving back at you. Upside: hide and seek with your nephews is over forever. You win every round. They hate you for it. And here's the hardest part. Maya. Everyone asks the same question. Boy or girl? You could find out in one glance. But Maya asked for one thing. Don't look. Not at the baby. Not once. Ultrasound is safe for babies because it uses sound, not radiation. Your eyes are not ultrasound. So you never look. Not even a peek. It's the hardest thing you've ever not done. Your mother-in-law calls every Sunday. Well? Did you look? No, Mom. Not even a little? Not even... a little. Maya's friends throw a baby shower with pink balloons on one side of the room and blue on the other. Everyone stares at you, like you're hiding the answer in your pocket. Are you? No... but you could be. And some nights, lying awake, you feel the baby kick against your back through the blanket. Tiny feet. Right there. One second would do it... One blink. You squeeze your eyes shut and count sheep instead. Forty-two sheep later, you're still awake... and still proud of yourself. Then a contractor sees you find a hidden safe inside a wall. He films it. The clip goes viral. And two weeks later, a man in a cowboy hat and a very white smile knocks on your door. His name is Gus Lane. He hosts a TV show called Treasure in the Walls. They tear open old buildings looking for hidden rooms, lost money and forgotten history. Mostly they find dead pigeons. Gus wants you on the show. Ten episodes. A house for you and Maya. Enough money that she could stay home with the baby as long as she likes. All you have to do is look. As long as the cameras need you to. The cameras need you to look... a lot. Maya reads the contract at the kitchen table. Her eyebrows climb higher with every page. Rio, it says unlimited scanning. Your badge will be red by lunch. You tell her you'll be careful. She doesn't answer. She just slides her hand onto her belly and looks out the window. Think bigger for a second. What if everyone could see through walls? There'd be no such thing as privacy. Builders would line every home with lead. Airports wouldn't need scanners. And every magician on Earth would be out of a job by Friday. The first episodes are great. You find a speakeasy hidden behind a bookshelf. A stash of old silver dollars inside a staircase. The ratings explode. Gus calls you the Human Scanner. But the badge turns orange more and more. Your eyes ache at night. And Gus keeps asking for one more look. One more angle. Hold it, Rio, hold it... we're losing the light. The season finale is live. An old warehouse by the river, rumored to hide a gangster's vault. A storm is moving in. And that's when the roof gives way. And that's where we started. Dust. Screams. A trapped camera operator named Luis under a pile of bricks. And a badge on your shirt that's almost red. Firefighters arrive in minutes. They don't know where to dig. Luis isn't answering. Gus is in your face. Look, Rio! Hold the look, it's the best TV we'll ever make! You could. You could stare into that rubble for five straight minutes, mapping every brick, live on television. But Luis is under there. And the firefighter crawling closest to him has no lead apron. Every second you stare... you're dosing them both. You need another way. Everything hangs on one decision. Stare into the rubble as long as it takes, while the cameras roll... or blink, step back, and do it Maya's way. You blink. You step back. Time, distance, shielding. Time first. You look in one-second glances. Blink. Look. Blink. Look. Like a camera flash instead of a floodlight. Distance next. You walk thirty feet away and look from there. The beam spreads out with distance, and the dose drops fast. Then shielding. You yell to the firefighters. Is there lead anywhere in this building? An old guy on the crew shouts back. The warehouse used to store car batteries. There are lead sheets in the back room. Perfect. They slide a sheet of lead over the rescuer's back. Then over Luis's chest, where the rubble is thinnest. Now your glances can pass through the bricks and stop at the shield. Blink. You see him. Left side, under a steel beam, one arm free. There's an air pocket. He's breathing. Blink. You see the safest place to lift. Twenty minutes later, they pull Luis out. Dusty. Shaken. Waving. The crowd cheers. Gus, for once, has nothing to say. The badge on your shirt? Still orange. Not red. That night, the hospital calls. Not about Luis. About Maya. The baby is coming early. You get there just in time. You keep your eyes closed the whole drive. Just in case. A few hours later, a nurse places a tiny, squirming bundle in your arms. It's a girl. And you found out the old way. With your own two eyes... and no beam at all. You name her Lena. Gus offers you season two. You say yes, with conditions. One look per room. A full lead-shielding crew. And a safety expert on set. Maya. So, could this really happen? Not the beam from your eyes. Human eyes only detect visible light, and they don't shoot anything out. But seeing through walls? Scientists are getting surprisingly close. In 1895, German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays by accident. Within weeks, he made an image of the bones inside his wife's hand, with her ring floating on one finger. In 2017, researchers used particles from space called muons to scan the Great Pyramid of Giza. They found a huge hidden empty space inside it that nobody knew existed. And today, some researchers can use ordinary Wi-Fi signals to sense people moving on the other side of a wall. So we can already see through stone. Just not with our eyes. And here's a mystery for you. That hidden space in the Great Pyramid is around a hundred feet long. Nobody has been inside it. Nobody knows what it's for. So what's in there? Would you have looked at the baby? Be honest, and drop the first thing you'd look through in the comments. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!
long.facts:
- X-rays pass through soft tissue, blocked by bone and metal
- X-rays can damage cells; dose depends on time
- Radiation workers wear dosimeter badges
- Radiation safety principles: time, distance, shielding; lead is used as shielding
- Ultrasound uses sound, not ionizing radiation
- Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and imaged his wife's hand with her ring
- 2017 ScanPyramids muon imaging found a large void in the Great Pyramid
- Wi-Fi signals can be used to sense motion behind walls
long.check:
- Size of pyramid void (reported at least ~30 m / ~100 ft)
- Dosimeter colors are a story device; real badges are read by labs, not color-coded

long.title: What If You Could Speak Every Language?
long.rel: Rio and his grandfather Lolo Ben, a Filipino immigrant whose memory is fading and who keeps slipping back into Ilocano (supporting: billionaire investor Grant Hale).
long.rule: Rio understands and speaks any language only when he hears one voice at a time; when several languages overlap, everything collapses into static, and the more he uses the power in a day, the longer the static lasts.
long.plant: Lolo Ben hums the old Ilocano folk song Pamulinawen whenever he is scared, the same song he hummed to Rio as a baby.
long.choice: Pick up the phone, listen in, and get rich... or let the money go and follow one old song through the noise.
long.script: The taxi driver outside your hotel is muttering in Amharic about the traffic. You lean in the window and answer him... in Amharic. He nearly drives onto the sidewalk. Then he laughs so hard he gives you a free ride. At the coffee cart, two tourists are arguing in Korean about whether the barista can understand them. He can't. You can. You tell them the oat milk is in the back. They turn the color of strawberries. And at the park, a toddler is babbling at a pigeon. Nonsense sounds. Baby talk. No language at all. And honestly... it's a relief. Because baby talk is the only thing left on Earth... you can't translate. Your name is Rio. You work the front desk at a busy hotel in Miami. Guests arrive from every corner of the world, all day long. And three weeks ago, you woke up understanding every language on the planet. Every single one. There are about seven thousand languages spoken today. Most people speak one or two. A few talented people speak five or six. You? You speak all of them. Fluently. With the right accent, the right slang... even the right jokes. Here's the strange part. You didn't learn anything. When someone speaks, the meaning just... blooms in your head. Like a flower opening. You answer, and the right words come out of your mouth. Your brain handles language in a few special areas, mostly on the left side. One region, called Broca's area, helps you build speech. Another, Wernicke's area, helps you understand it. Yours seem to be working overtime. But there's a rule. It only works with one voice at a time. When two or more languages overlap, they crash together into static. Like twenty radios playing at once. You hear the sounds, but the meaning disappears. And the more you use the power during the day, the longer the static lasts. In the morning, a crowded room fuzzes out for a few seconds. By night... it can last for minutes. So what if you could speak every language? Upside: your hotel loves you. A family from Brazil can't find their passports. You sort it out in Portuguese in two minutes. A businessman from Japan has a dinner reservation problem. Fixed... in perfect Japanese. A grandmother from Ukraine just wants to tell someone about her grandkids. You listen for twenty minutes. In Ukrainian. Your manager gives you employee of the month. Then employee of the year. Then a raise. Upside: menus. Every restaurant in Miami suddenly has a secret menu. The cook at the Peruvian place starts making you dishes that aren't on the board. The lady at the Vietnamese bakery slips you an extra pastry and tells you which of her sons is her favorite. You will take that secret to your grave. Downside: you hear everything. Every whispered complaint. Every rude comment people think nobody understands. The couple in room four twelve? They think the lobby smells like old cheese. They're not wrong. Upside: you can finally talk to your grandfather. Lolo Ben moved to Miami from the Philippines fifty years ago. He learned English. He spoke it at work, at church, at your baseball games. But lately, his memory is slipping. And when it slips, his English slips with it. He drifts back into Ilocano, the language he grew up speaking in his village. Doctors see this in some bilingual people with dementia. Newer languages fade first. The first language... stays longest. For two years, your family has watched Lolo talk and talk... and nobody could understand him. Your mom would nod and hold his hand. You'd smile and pretend. Now you sit beside him on the porch. Lolo, you say in Ilocano. Tell me about the village. His eyes go wide. Then wet. And then he talks for three hours. About his mother's rice fields. About the river. About a girl named Celia who threw a mango at his head. He married her. That was your grandmother. Upside: the best three hours of your life. And one thing you remember from those talks. When Lolo gets scared, he hums. Always the same song. An old Ilocano folk song called Pamulinawen. He hummed it to you when you were a baby. You didn't know the name until now. He still hums it during thunderstorms. During doctor visits. During the news. Then it happens. A hotel guest films you switching between eight languages in one minute. The clip goes everywhere. And a billionaire calls. His name is Grant Hale. He makes deals all over the world, worth billions of dollars. He wants you at his side. Officially, as his translator. Unofficially? He wants you to listen when the other side whispers to each other. In their own language. When they think nobody understands. You'd hear their real price. Their real plans. Their secrets. Grant offers you more money each week than you earn in a year. Is it wrong? Nobody would know. You'd just be... listening. You tell your mom. She frowns. Rio, that's spying. You tell Lolo. He doesn't say anything. He just hums. Now think bigger. What if everyone woke up speaking every language? Every textbook would be rewritten overnight. Spies would be useless. The internet would explode with jokes nobody could understand before. And for the first time in history... every human on Earth could argue with every other human, directly. Would that be peace... or chaos? Grant gives you a test. A phone call. Tonight. A secret meeting with a company from Germany, and you'll listen in. If it works, the job is yours. But tonight there's a problem. A hurricane is heading toward Miami. A big one. The city orders evacuations. Your family's neighborhood is in the flood zone. You drive Lolo and your mom to a shelter in a high school gym. And it's packed. Hundreds of families. Haitian Creole. Spanish. Portuguese. Russian. Vietnamese. Babies crying. Radios blaring. Rain hammering the roof. For you... it's static. Pure static. You've used the power all day at the hotel. The static is thick. Then the lights flicker and go out. When the backup lights come on... Lolo is gone. Your mom is frantic. He was right here! You run through the gym. Hundreds of faces. Hundreds of voices. You try to ask people if they've seen an old man, but they answer in a dozen languages at once. All of it melts into noise. Then your phone rings. It's Grant. Rio, the Germans are on the line. Pick up and listen. This is your test. Right now. And here's the thing. A phone call is one voice at a time. It would work perfectly. You could hear every secret. You could get rich... tonight. But Lolo is out there. Somewhere in the dark. Confused. Scared. Now you have to decide. Pick up the phone, listen in, and get rich... or let the money go and follow one old song through the noise. You hang up on a billionaire. And then you stop. You stand perfectly still in the middle of the gym. You stop trying to understand the words. You stop listening for meaning. Because meaning isn't working tonight. You listen for music. Babies. Radios. Thunder. Hundreds of voices... And there. Faint. Under all of it. A melody. Low. Shaky. Pamulinawen. You follow it. Past the bleachers. Past the vending machines. Down a dark hallway. Into the boys' locker room. Lolo is sitting on a bench, wet from a leaky pipe, holding his cane, humming to himself. Like he hummed to you, a long time ago. You sit down beside him. And you hum with him. He looks up. Rio? You found me. In English. Clear as day. Yeah, Lolo. You taught me how. You walk him back to your mom. She cries. He tells her not to cry... in Ilocano. And this time, you translate. The storm passes by morning. Your house floods a little. The porch survives. So does Lolo. Grant Hale never calls back. You don't miss him. A few weeks later, the hospital where Lolo sees his doctors asks if you'd volunteer. Patients from all over the world come there, scared and confused, and many of them can't explain what hurts. One voice at a time... that's perfect for you. Two days a week, you sit with patients and doctors and make sure they understand each other. And on Sundays, you sit on the porch with Lolo. He tells stories. You write them down. In Ilocano. For your future kids. How much of this is real? Speaking every language? No. But some people get surprisingly close. In the 1800s, an Italian cardinal named Giuseppe Mezzofanti was famous for speaking dozens of languages. Some accounts say more than thirty. Visitors from all over the world tested him. Most left amazed. And here's a real superpower everyone is born with. Very young babies can tell apart speech sounds from every language on Earth. By around their first birthday, they get better at the sounds of their own language... and slowly lose the others. Every human starts as a universal listener. And today, earbuds can translate conversations almost in real time. Not perfectly. But fast. Here's a mystery for you, though. There's a medieval book called the Voynich manuscript. It's filled with strange writing and drawings of plants nobody can identify. Scientists dated its pages to the early 1400s. To this day, nobody can read a single sentence. Even with your power... could you? Your power only works for spoken words. So which language would you speak first? And is there someone in your family whose stories you wish you understood? long.facts:
- About 7,000 languages spoken today
- Broca's area (speech production) and Wernicke's area (comprehension), mostly left hemisphere
- Some bilingual people with dementia revert to their first language
- Pamulinawen is a traditional Ilocano folk song
- Cardinal Giuseppe Mezzofanti (1800s) reportedly spoke dozens of languages
- Young infants can distinguish speech sounds of all languages; narrows by around the first birthday
- Real-time translation earbuds exist
- Voynich manuscript carbon-dated to early 1400s and still undeciphered

- Perceptual narrowing age (roughly 6-12 months)

long.title: What If You Always Knew When Someone Was Lying?
long.rel: Rio and his father Ray, a proud retired firefighter in Phoenix who never admits he's hurt (supporting: poker pro Vince Calloway).
long.rule: Rio hears a sharp buzz whenever a speaker knows they're lying, but it never tells him why, honest mistakes pass silently, and kind lies buzz just as loudly as cruel ones.
long.plant: Since Rio was little, Ray has used one family check-in whenever someone gets hurt: 'Give me a number, one to ten.'
long.choice: Stay in your seat and play the eight million dollar hand... or stand up, walk out, and make the call.
long.script: The final table in Las Vegas is so quiet, you can hear the ice melting in someone's glass. Eight million dollars in chips sit in the middle. The man across from you pushes everything in. He looks you dead in the eye and says, I've got you beat. And in your head... nothing. No buzz. He's telling the truth. You should fold. You know you should fold. But your phone is buzzing in your pocket. Not a buzz in your head... a real one. It's your dad. You step back from the table for ten seconds and answer. Dad? I'm fine, son. Just calling to say good luck. And right there, in your head, the buzz screams like a smoke alarm. He's lying. Three hundred miles away... your father is lying to you. Why? Let's back up. Your name is Rio. You sell used cars in Phoenix, Arizona. And four months ago, you started hearing lies. Not seeing them. Hearing them. Every time someone says something they know is false, a sharp buzz goes off inside your head. Like a mosquito in your ear. Loud ones for big lies. Little ones for small lies. And here's the thing. You never knew how much people lie. Researchers have found that people tell small lies pretty often... many people report about one or two a day. And they're mostly tiny. I love the sweater. I'm five minutes away. No, you didn't wake me up. Your phone buzzes... I mean your head buzzes... all day long. Most people are terrible at catching lies. In big reviews of lie detection studies, people guessed right only about fifty-four percent of the time. That's barely better than flipping a coin. You? One hundred percent. Every time. There's just one rule. And it's tricky. The buzz only fires when someone knows they're lying. If they believe something false, it stays silent. Honest mistakes don't buzz. Bad memories don't buzz. And it never tells you why someone is lying. A kind lie and a cruel lie buzz exactly the same. So what if you always knew when someone was lying? At work, it's incredible. At first. A customer swears the car he's trading in has never been in an accident. Buzz. You check under the hood. Bent frame. A coworker says he didn't take your lunch from the fridge. Buzz. He has turkey on his chin. Your boss says the dealership is doing great this month. Buzz. Hmm. Upside: you're the best salesman on the lot. You know when a customer is bluffing about a lower price across town. Downside: you also know when your manager is bluffing about your bonus. Upside: no more scams. That email from a prince who needs your bank details? Your head doesn't buzz at emails. But the phone call from the fake bank? Buzzing like a beehive. Downside: dates. Oh no. Dates. I love hiking... buzz. I'm not on my phone much... buzz. I'm thirty-two... buzz buzz. You start staying home on Friday nights. With pizza. Pizza never lies. Then there's the worst part. You can't turn it off. Your best friend, Marco, shows you his new tattoo. It's a wolf. It looks... like a potato with ears. Do you like it? You open your mouth to say yes... and you realize something. You can't hear your own lies. But you know they're lies. And now that you hear everyone else's... yours feel louder somehow. So you say it. It's a potato, Marco. He doesn't talk to you for a week. Is honesty always kind? Or is it sometimes just... rude? You start learning a new skill. Not lying... just choosing what to say. It's a cool idea, man. The wolf has spirit. No buzz. Not from you, anyway. And here's the other surprise. Most of the buzzes you hear every day? They're not mean. They're nervous. People lie about being fine. About being busy. About not caring. The lies that hurt the most... are the ones people tell to protect themselves. And then there's your dad. Ray. Thirty years as a Phoenix firefighter. Big hands. Bigger laugh. Never takes a day off. Never admits he's hurt. When you were seven, you fell off your bike and split your knee open. You were crying so hard you couldn't talk. Your dad knelt down and asked you one question. Give me a number, Rio. One to ten. How bad? Seven, you sobbed. Okay, he said. Seven means we go see the doctor. That became your family thing. Broken arm? Give me a number. Bad day at school? Give me a number. Heartbreak at sixteen? Your dad sat on the edge of your bed. Number? Nine, you said. He sat with you until midnight. The only person who never gave a real number... was him. Dad, how's your back? I'm fine. Buzz. Dad, did the doctor call? Not yet. Buzz. You never push. That's just Dad. Then a customer recognizes your talent. He's not buying a car. He's a professional poker player named Vince Calloway. He watched you call a dozen bluffs on the sales lot. He laughs. Kid, do you play cards? Two months later, you're sitting at a poker table in Las Vegas. Vince is sponsoring you. He pays the entry fees. You split the winnings. Is it cheating? You tell yourself it isn't. Poker is a game of reading people. You just read them... better. Way better. You win. Then you win again. Then you make the final table of the biggest tournament of the year. Top prize? Eight million dollars. Vince is giddy. Your coworkers at the dealership watch on TV. Your dad calls before you leave. Proud of you, son. No buzz. That one was real. Now imagine a world where everyone could hear lies. Would courtrooms disappear? Would politicians go silent? Would surprise parties be dead forever? And what about the little lies that keep people kind? I love your cooking, Grandma. Would anyone ever say it again? Back at the final table. Eight hours of play. Three players left. Then two. You and a quiet man from Texas. And that's when your dad calls. And that's when he says I'm fine. And that's when your head screams. You step away from the table. The tournament director frowns. Sir, you have sixty seconds to return. You cover your other ear. Dad, what's going on? Nothing. Just a little indigestion. Buzz. Where are you? Home. Watching you on TV. No buzz. Then the question comes out of your mouth before you even think. Give me a number, Dad. One to ten. There's a long pause. Two. The buzz is so loud you almost drop the phone. Your dad isn't watching a poker game with indigestion. Your dad is hurting. Badly. And hiding it so he doesn't ruin your big night. Chest pain. Pressure. Maybe pain spreading to the arm or the jaw. Those can be signs of a heart attack. And many people, especially tough people, wait too long. They don't want to make a fuss. The tournament director is waving at you. Vince is mouthing, sit down, sit down. Eight million dollars is waiting on that table. But your dad is alone, three hundred miles away. It's down to one decision. Stay in your seat and play the eight million dollar hand... or stand up, walk out, and make the call. You walk out. Behind you, the director announces a forfeit. You don't hear it. You're already dialing. First, nine one one. You give them your dad's address in Phoenix. They send an ambulance. Then you call your dad's neighbor, Mrs. Delgado. She has a key. She runs across the yard in her slippers. Then you call your dad back and stay on the line. Dad. Listen to me. Help is coming. Unlock the front door. Sit down. Don't drive anywhere. I'm fine, son. Buzz. Dad... I can hear it. There's a long silence. Then his voice cracks. Okay. Okay... it's an eight. Thank you, you whisper. Thank you for the real number. You hear the sirens arrive through the phone. You hear Mrs. Delgado telling the paramedics to hurry. And you hear your dad say one last thing before they take the phone. Don't you dare feel bad about the money. No buzz. It was a heart attack. The paramedics got there in nine minutes. The doctors opened a blocked artery that night. Every minute counted. Your dad is going to be okay. You drive home through the desert at sunrise. Vince calls you twice. You don't pick up. The third time, he leaves a message. I watched the replay, kid. You walked away from eight million bucks. Buzz? No. You're crazy... but you're right. Eight days later, you're sitting beside your dad's hospital bed. He's pale. Grumpy. Alive. The nurse asks how his pain is today. He glances at you. Then he sighs. Three. No buzz. She smiles and writes it down. You go back to selling cars. You still hear every lie. But you stop treating every buzz like a crime. Some people lie because they're scared. Some because they're kind. And some, like your dad... because they love you too much to worry you. And the poker? You never play again. But here's what's been keeping you awake. Last week, you watched an old interview with yourself. From your first day on the sales lot. Before the power. You said, I love this job. And through the TV speakers... something buzzed. Was it you? Or was it someone in the room behind the camera? Who do you know who always says I'm fine? Send this to them, and tell us in the comments: would you rather hear every lie, or none? Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!
long.facts:
- Many people report telling about one or two lies a day, mostly small (DePaulo diary studies)
- People detect lies only about 54% of the time on average (Bond and DePaulo 2006 meta-analysis)
- Heart attack warning signs: chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to arm or jaw, shortness of breath
- Many people delay calling for help during heart attack symptoms
- Call 911, unlock the door, don't drive yourself
- Pain scale 0/1-10 used in medicine
long.check:
- 'One or two lies a day' (diary-study average; distribution is skewed)
- 54% lie detection accuracy figure

long.title: What If You Could Shrink To One Inch Tall?
long.rel: Rio and Mrs. Okafor, a retired watchmaker in her seventies who owns the tiny repair shop where Rio works and treats him like a son (supporting: Dr. Pike from a defense contractor).
long.rule: Rio can shrink to one inch tall, but a tiny body gains and loses heat very fast, so he can only stay small for about fifteen minutes in normal weather, and far less in heat or cold.
long.plant: Mrs. Okafor sews Rio a tiny jacket out of a scrap of silver emergency blanket, the kind that reflects heat.
long.choice: Walk through those glass doors and sign... or shrink down in a hundred-degree parking lot.
long.script: You drop your car keys between the seat and the center console. Most people need a flashlight, a coat hanger and five minutes of swearing. You? You shrink. One inch tall. You stroll down into the crack, step over a fossilized french fry, grab the key ring, and climb back up. Total time? Twenty seconds. At the repair shop, a customer brings in an old music box that hasn't played in forty years. Mrs. Okafor sighs. Something's jammed deep inside. You wait until she turns around. You shrink, crawl through the keyhole, and find it. A single grain of rice, wedged in the gears. Who put a grain of rice in a music box? A mystery for another day. When she turns back, the music box is playing. Mrs. Okafor narrows her eyes at you. You whistle innocently. And at home, your cat has found a new hobby. Hunting you. You've learned to shrink only in the bathroom. With the door locked. Your name is Rio. You live in Seattle and work at a tiny repair shop that fixes watches, clocks, radios and anything with gears. And two months ago, you sneezed... and shrank. One inch tall. About the size of a paper clip. You weigh about as much as a jelly bean. Now, this should be impossible. When animals get smaller, everything about their bodies changes. And the biggest change? Heat. Here's why. Your body makes heat inside and loses it through your skin. Shrink down, and your outside surface becomes huge compared to your inside. Tiny animals lose heat crazy fast. That's why the smallest mammals, like shrews, eat almost constantly. Some shrews have to eat every few hours, or they starve. Their tiny hearts race at over a thousand beats every minute. That's your rule. Small you is a little furnace with no walls. In normal room temperature, you can stay tiny for about fifteen minutes before you start shivering uncontrollably. In the cold? Five minutes. In heat? Your body warms up just as fast. It cuts both ways. So what if you could shrink to one inch tall? Upside: you find every lost earring in Seattle. Upside: free rides. Pigeons. Buses. Your coworker's backpack. Downside: rain. In Seattle. Every raindrop is the size of a bowling ball to you. One hit, and you're flat on the sidewalk, soaked and mad. Upside: you're terrifyingly strong. For your size. Muscle strength depends on how thick your muscles are. Your weight depends on your whole volume. When you shrink, your weight drops much faster than your strength. That's why ants can carry many times their own body weight. You? You can lift a sugar cube over your head and do a little victory dance. Downside: your voice. Tiny vocal cords vibrate fast, so when you talk, you sound like a mouse who just inhaled helium. Mrs. Okafor laughs so hard she has to sit down. Mrs. Okafor owns the shop. She's seventy-four, from Lagos, and she was a watchmaker for fifty years. Her hands are steady as a surgeon's. Her eyes are not what they used to be. She hired you when you were nineteen and broke, and she's been feeding you lunch ever since. Jollof rice every Friday. You're not allowed to say no. She's the only person you've told. On the first day you told her, she didn't freak out. She just held up a magnifying glass and squinted. You'll freeze to death, little man... in this city? In this rain? Then she went to her sewing kit. She cut a scrap from a silver emergency blanket, the crinkly kind runners wear after a marathon. And she stitched you a tiny jacket. Smaller than a stamp. Wear this every time, she said. It holds your heat in. And it bounces heat away when the sun is hot. Those blankets reflect warmth like a mirror. You laughed. It looks like a potato chip bag. But you wore it. Every time. Then you get noticed. A clock collector catches you on camera climbing out of a grandfather clock. The video is shaky, blurry... and goes everywhere. A week later, a woman in a sharp gray suit walks into the shop. Dr. Pike. She works for a defense contractor in Virginia. She's very polite and very serious. We have machines worth billions of dollars, Rio. Satellites. Jet engines. Some parts are so tiny and so deep inside, we have to take the whole thing apart to fix them. You could just... walk in. She slides a folder across the counter. A salary five times what you make now. A house. A secret program. You can't tell anyone what you do. Ever. Not even Mrs. Okafor. And you'd leave Seattle in a week. Mrs. Okafor reads the folder over your shoulder. Then she goes back to her workbench without a word. That night, she doesn't make jollof rice. That's how you know she's upset. Now picture a whole world of one-inch people. A single pizza would feed a city block for a week. A flight to Europe would cost a few pennies. Cats would be the most dangerous animals on Earth. And a puddle? A puddle would be a lake with a lifeguard. Dr. Pike sets up a meeting. Phoenix, Arizona. Their testing center. You fly down to sign the papers. It's July. It's one hundred eleven degrees. The parking lot is a frying pan. You're walking toward the glass doors with Dr. Pike when you hear it. A tiny, weak cry. From a silver car parked in the sun. You look through the window. A baby. Maybe a year old. Strapped in a car seat in the back. Red faced. Sweaty. Barely crying anymore. The doors are locked. No parent in sight. On a hot day, the inside of a car can heat up about twenty degrees in just ten minutes. Babies heat up much faster than adults. Their small bodies can't cool down well. Sound familiar? Dr. Pike is already on her phone. I'll call security. And nine one one. We're late, Rio. They'll handle it. Will they? The fire station could be ten minutes away. The baby may not have ten minutes. The car's back window is cracked open. Half an inch. Just enough. For you. But it's one hundred eleven degrees out here. And inside that car? Way hotter. A one-inch body in an oven heats up in seconds. You might last a minute. Maybe less. It comes down to this. Walk through those glass doors and sign... or shrink down in a hundred-degree parking lot. You pull the tiny silver jacket out of your wallet. Dr. Pike stares at you. Is that... a potato chip bag? You shrink. The heat slams into you like a wall. The pavement burns through your shoes... like walking on a stovetop. You run across a parking lot that feels as big as a desert. Ten feet to the car. To you... that's a football field. A gust of hot wind knocks you sideways. A bottle cap rolls past like a runaway wheel. Keep going... keep going. You climb the hot tire. You leap for the window gap. The silver jacket flashes in the sun, bouncing back the worst of it. Inside the car, the air is so thick and hot it feels like breathing soup. You land on the back seat. Your heart is hammering. Your vision is going sparkly. And then you do the only thing you can. You grow. Back to full size. Right there in the back seat, squashed next to a car seat, your head bent against the roof. You reach over, pop the lock, and throw open the door. Cool air. Well, hot air. But cooler. You unbuckle the baby and carry her into the shade of the building. Dr. Pike runs in and comes back with cold water and wet towels. The paramedics arrive four minutes later. They take over, cooling her down gently. One of them looks at you. You got her out just in time. The mom comes sprinting across the lot. She left the baby for one quick errand. She thought the baby was asleep at home with her husband. He thought she had her. A terrible mix-up. It happens to loving parents more often than anyone wants to believe. Dr. Pike watches you sitting on the curb, red faced, sweat pouring, still holding that silver jacket. Then she tears the contract in half. Not because you failed. Because she has a better idea. Six months later, you're back in Seattle. Mrs. Okafor's shop has a new sign. Okafor and Rio, Tiny Repairs. Dr. Pike's company sends you one job a month. You fly out, do it, and fly home by Friday. Just in time for jollof rice. And Mrs. Okafor has started a new project. A whole row of tiny silver jackets. One for every season. Okay... real or not? Not shrinking. A human squished to one inch would have a brain smaller than a pea, and nowhere to fit eighty-six billion neurons. But the science of small is very real. The Etruscan shrew, one of the smallest mammals on Earth, weighs about as much as a paper clip. Its heart can beat over one thousand times a minute. And ants can carry objects many times heavier than themselves, because of the same strength math that helped you. Doctors are going small too. Surgeons already use robots with tiny tools to operate through cuts smaller than a fingernail. Scientists are even testing micro-robots that could swim through the body one day. But here's what nobody can answer yet. If you were one inch tall... would time feel slower? Some small animals take in the world faster than we do. A fly sees motion so quickly that a rolled-up newspaper looks slow. So would tiny you live in slow motion too? What would you do first at one inch tall? And who is your Mrs. Okafor? Tell us in the comments. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!
long.facts:
- Smaller bodies have more surface area per volume and lose or gain heat faster
- Shrews must eat almost constantly; heart rates above 1,000 bpm
- Muscle strength scales with cross-section, weight with volume, so small animals are relatively stronger (ants)
- Emergency (Mylar) blankets reflect radiant heat
- A car interior can heat about 20 F in 10 minutes; children overheat faster than adults
- Children left in hot cars often result from parental mix-ups
- Human brain has about 86 billion neurons
- Etruscan shrew weighs about as much as a paper clip (~1.8 g); heart rate over 1,000 bpm
- Robotic surgery through small incisions; research on micro-robots
- Flies perceive motion faster than humans (higher flicker fusion rate)
long.check:
- '20 F in 10 minutes' car heating (NHTSA / San Jose State data)
- Etruscan shrew heart rate (reported up to ~1,500 bpm)
- Mylar blanket heat reflection claim is fine; use in hot sun simplified

long.title: What If You Grew To 20 Feet Tall?
long.rel: Rio and his twin brother Leo, who run the family corn farm in Iowa together (supporting: film director Simone Vance).
long.rule: Rio can grow to twenty feet for up to an hour, but his weight grows about thirty-seven times while his bones only get about eleven times stronger, so running, jumping or a fall can snap his legs.
long.plant: Leo's two-note whistle, from the days their grandpa taught them to move cattle: 'Slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.'
long.choice: Sprint for the cameras like a real monster... or slow down to the speed of an old tractor and trust your brother.
long.script: The creek has swallowed the road. Brown water roars over the low crossing, two feet deep and rising. In the middle of it, a yellow school bus sits tilted, its front wheels stuck in mud. Nineteen kids are pressed against the windows. The driver is on the radio, but the fire trucks are stuck on the other side of the flood. Behind you, a movie crew is still filming. Hand therapists often say your pinky and ring finger provide much of your grip strength. Lose the pinky, and your grip gets noticeably weaker. And the answer? Each hand has twenty-seven bones. Together, your hands and wrists hold more than a quarter of all the bones in your body. Did you guess that many? Subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

shorts.title: What If You Couldn't Smell Your Own House?
shorts.topic: Nose blindness (olfactory adaptation)
shorts.hook: Your friends are standing in your doorway, holding their noses, and you have no idea why.
shorts.script: Your friends are standing in your doorway, holding their noses, and you have no idea why. You're Rio, and to you, your apartment smells like nothing. Let's rewind. Two weeks ago, you adopted a dog named Pickles. You also started cooking a lot of fish. And you stopped taking out the trash on time. The smell grew. You noticed less. What happened? It's called nose blindness. Scientists call it olfactory adaptation. When a smell stays around you all the time, your brain slowly stops paying attention to it. Your brain decides the smell is old news, so it can focus on new smells, like smoke or spoiled food. That's why everyone's home has a smell they can't notice. And it's why stepping outside for a few minutes, then walking back in, can help you smell it again. Your friend Tomas still makes you open every window. What does your home smell like to visitors? shorts.fact: Olfactory adaptation: the brain tunes out constant odors to detect new ones; leaving and returning can reset perception

Your brain is amazing at picking one voice out of a noisy room. Scientists studied this in the 1950s. People focused on one conversation could still notice when someone else said their name. Your brain is always listening in the background for things that matter to you. And your name matters most. So sometimes it jumps the gun. Rhino. Radio. Rio. Close enough. So I'm not crazy? shorts.title: What If Your Nose Bled Every Day?
shorts.topic: Why nosebleeds happen and the right way to stop one

shorts.script: You're in the middle of a job interview, and you feel something warm on your lip. You're Rio, and your interviewer, Ms. Lopez, hands you a tissue. Your nose bleeds every day now. Why do noses bleed so easily? The inside of your nose is lined with lots of tiny blood vessels, very close to the surface. Dry air, picking or a bump can break them. Most nosebleeds come from the front of the nose and aren't serious. Here's the lesson. Most people do it wrong. Don't tilt your head back. That sends blood down your throat. Instead, sit up and lean slightly forward. Pinch the soft part of your nose, just below the bony bridge, and hold it for ten to fifteen minutes without letting go to check. If it won't stop after about twenty minutes, or it follows a hard hit, get medical help. Send this to someone who still tilts their head back. Subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!
shorts.fact: The nasal lining has many surface vessels; most nosebleeds are anterior; first aid: lean forward, pinch the soft part for 10-15 minutes, don't tilt back; seek help if over ~20 minutes or after injury

shorts.title: What If You Could Only Eat Upside Down?
shorts.topic: How swallowing works without gravity
shorts.hook: You sit down to breakfast, and your cereal won't go down.
shorts.script: You sit down to breakfast, and your cereal won't go down. It just sits in your mouth. Your name is Rio, and you can only swallow when you're upside down. There's one rule. Tell anyone why, and it's permanent. So you start hanging off the couch at breakfast. Your roommate Jasper finds you dangling from the monkey bars at the park, eating a sandwich. Wait... can people even swallow upside down? Yes. Your food doesn't just fall into your stomach. Muscles in your esophagus squeeze in waves, pushing food along, like toothpaste through a tube. It's called peristalsis. That's why astronauts can eat and drink in space, with no gravity at all. Your body pushes the food down... or up... no matter which way you're pointing. Then Jasper asks Dude... why are you eating like a bat? And you almost tell him. Almost. Would you have told him the truth? Subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!
shorts.fact: Peristalsis moves food through the esophagus in waves regardless of gravity, which is why astronauts can eat and drink in space
